result.markdown: # Interlude: Attention as Test-Time Regression {#sec-interlude-test-time-regression} During autoregressive generation, a causal Transformer can retain the keys and values of earlier tokens in a key--value (KV) cache, described in the [architectural trade-offs](../part4/14-self-attention-transformer.qmd#what-the-architecture-bought) section of @sec-14-self-attention-transformer, so that each new query attends to all prior tokens without recomputing them. This interlude compares three ways to construct that memory computation: a query-local fit over stored pairs, running statistics for a factorized kernel, and an online linear predictor updated by the delta rule. Read this way, attention is an online regression estimator at test time. The constructions share a regression perspective, but they need not solve the same optimization problem. Softmax attention, linear attention, state-space models and DeltaNet differ in the kernel, the predictor class, the regularization and the update rule, and these choices determine both the answer and the information that must be retained. ## Three memory constructions through regression {#one-regression-three-solvers} The recurrent networks of @sec-10-sequences-rnn compressed the history into a fixed-size state. The Transformer resolved that bottleneck by keeping the visible key--value rows available. Reading those rows becomes more expensive as the prefix grows, and across a complete sequence dense routing has quadratic cost. There is another resolution: return to the regression perspective of @sec-12-kernel-regression and change the kernel, the predictor class, or the update rule. Some of these choices permit a state of fixed size. Recent sequence models make that move under names such as test-time regression, test-time training, fast weights, linear attention, DeltaNet, Titans, MesaNet, and state-space sequence models. Each solver is characterized by what information it retains and what computational trade-offs it accepts. ### Choices within the regression framework {#one-objective-four-dials} At time $t$, let learned projections turn each token representation $\vect{x}_\tau$ into two views, $$ \vect{k}_\tau=\matr{W}_K\vect{x}_\tau, \qquad \vect{v}_\tau=\matr{W}_V\vect{x}_\tau. $$ Following [Wang, Shi, and Fox (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12352), we describe memory construction as a weighted regression problem. A memory layer builds an online predictor $M_t:\mathbb{R}^{d_k}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d_v}$: $$ M_t =\arg\min_{M\in\mathcal{M}} \frac{1}{2}\sum_{\tau\le t}w_{t,\tau} \norm{M(\vect{k}_\tau)-\vect{v}_\tau}^{2} +\Omega(M), \qquad \vect{y}_t=M_t(\vect{q}_t), \quad \vect{q}_t=\matr{W}_Q\vect{x}_t. $$ The display specifies a reference fitting problem. An online update need not attain its minimizer. Query-local attention also makes the observation weights depend on the query, as the next construction shows. Here the keys and values are computed from the input sequence. The memory state changes during the forward computation, while the projection parameters are held fixed during that evaluation. The frame exposes four design choices. **The views.** $\matr{W}_Q,\matr{W}_K,\matr{W}_V$ are the learned projections of @sec-14-self-attention-transformer: queries and keys are compared, and values are what the comparison passes on. The token is not assigned one permanent meaning. The three projections give it a query, a key that provides the features used for comparison, and a value. **The history weights.** $w_{t,\tau}$ determine how much an older residual matters to the fitting problem. The forget gates of @sec-10-sequences-rnn already made retention depend on time and content. A geometric schedule can privilege recent errors; an input-dependent schedule can keep some tokens longer than others. **The model and regularizer.** The class $\mathcal{M}$ determines whether the predictor is a local constant, a linear map, or something richer. $\Omega$ brings back ridge penalties from @sec-01-linear-regression and weight decay from @sec-04-training-loss-sgd. Regularization controls the fitted map. It is not, by itself, the same operation as forgetting old observations. **The solver.** A closed-form local fit, a running sufficient statistic, and one gradient step do different work and preserve different information. A layer may compute a closed-form solution or execute an iterative or approximate update, whose rule may itself be learned. This objective is an umbrella, not an equivalence theorem. Its methods can restrict different function classes, use different weights, and stop at different approximations. ### Solver 1: keep the data and fit at the query Softmax attention instantiates the framework as a query-local constant estimator. For a query $\vect{q}$, the predictor class $\mathcal{M}$ is restricted to constant vectors $\vect{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_v}$, and observation weights are the query-dependent affinities, yielding the local-constant problem $$ \vect{c}^{*}(\vect{q}) =\arg\min_{\vect{c}} \frac{1}{2}\sum_{\tau\le t} \kappa(\vect{q},\vect{k}_\tau) \norm{\vect{c}-\vect{v}_\tau}^{2}. $$ Write $\kappa_\tau=\kappa(\vect{q},\vect{k}_\tau)$. Differentiation gives $$ \nabla_{\vect{c}}= \sum_{\tau\le t}\kappa_\tau(\vect{c}-\vect{v}_\tau)=\vect{0} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \vect{c}^{*}= \frac{\sum_\tau\kappa_\tau\vect{v}_\tau}{\sum_\tau\kappa_\tau}. $$ Choose $\kappa(\vect{q},\vect{k})=\exp(\vect{q}^{\top}\vect{k}/\sqrt{d_k})$ and the normalized coefficients form a row of scaled dot-product softmax. The kernel supplies the weights, and the constant fit supplies the average. An unrestricted $M$ with unit observation weights and no regularizer would instead interpolate compatible training pairs and be undetermined away from them. We can check numerically that the gradient vanishes at the weighted average. Subtracting the largest score rescales every $\kappa_\tau$ by the same positive constant and leaves the minimizer unchanged. :::: {.plan-code} ::: {.plan} 1. Draw 12 seeded key-value pairs and a query, then form the weighted average, softmax output, and gradient. 2. Verify softmax attention's local-constant optimum. 3. Print the largest absolute entry of the stationarity gradient. ::: ::: {#local-constant-attention-check .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false" code-summary="Code: verify softmax attention's local-constant optimum"} # [1] ms_rng = np.random.default_rng(6050) ms_d, ms_T = 8, 12 ms_K = ms_rng.standard_normal((ms_T, ms_d)) ms_V = ms_rng.standard_normal((ms_T, 3)) ms_q = ms_rng.standard_normal(ms_d) ms_scores = ms_K @ ms_q / np.sqrt(ms_d) ms_kappa = np.exp(ms_scores - ms_scores.max()) ms_c = (ms_kappa[:, None] * ms_V).sum(0) / ms_kappa.sum() ms_attention = (ms_kappa / ms_kappa.sum()) @ ms_V ms_gradient = (ms_kappa[:, None] * (ms_c - ms_V)).sum(0) # [2] assert np.allclose(ms_c, ms_attention) # [3] print(f"max |stationarity gradient|: {np.abs(ms_gradient).max():.3e}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` max |stationarity gradient|: 3.053e-16 ``` ::: ::: :::: This solver retains the key--value rows because a future query may weight every row differently. That is why dense causal attention carries a growing dataset forward. ### Solver 2: collapse a factorized kernel into sufficient state Suppose the kernel factors through a finite feature map $\phi:\mathbb{R}^{d_k}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{r}$: $$ \kappa(\vect{q},\vect{k}) =\phi(\vect{q})^{\top}\phi(\vect{k}). $$ Assume the resulting kernel is nonnegative on the pairs being used and that the normalization denominator is positive. The positive feature map used below satisfies these conditions. Substitute that factorization into the weighted average and regroup terms: $$ \begin{aligned} \vect{y}_t(\vect{q}) &=\frac{\sum_{\tau\le t} \bigl[\phi(\vect{q})^{\top}\phi(\vect{k}_\tau)\bigr]\vect{v}_\tau} {\sum_{\tau\le t}\phi(\vect{q})^{\top}\phi(\vect{k}_\tau)} \\ &=\frac{\matr{S}_t^\top\phi(\vect{q})} {\vect{z}_t^\top\phi(\vect{q})}, \qquad \matr{S}_t\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times d_v}, \quad \vect{z}_t\in\mathbb{R}^{r}, \end{aligned} $$ where $$ \matr{S}_t=\sum_{\tau\le t}\phi(\vect{k}_\tau)\vect{v}_\tau^{\top}, \qquad \vect{z}_t=\sum_{\tau\le t}\phi(\vect{k}_\tau). $$ The sufficient state is the pair $(\matr{S}_t,\vect{z}_t)$, not $\matr{S}_t$ alone: the numerator needs accumulated value-weighted features and the denominator needs its normalizer. Each new pair updates that fixed-size state once. For this factorized kernel, any later query gets the same answer from the state as from a full traversal of all pairs. :::: {.plan-code} ::: {.plan} 1. Define the reusable `ms_phi` helper. 2. Initialize the sufficient-state pair, `ms_S` and `ms_z`, as zero arrays. 3. Compare a factorized-kernel traversal with its running state. 4. Check the claimed identities, shapes, or invariants. 5. Print whether `ms_streaming` matches `ms_traversal` and their largest absolute difference. ::: ::: {#linear-attention-sufficient-state-check .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false" code-summary="Code: compare a factorized-kernel traversal with its running state"} # [1] def ms_phi(x): return np.where(x > 0, x + 1, np.exp(x)) # [2] ms_S = np.zeros((ms_d, ms_V.shape[1])) ms_z = np.zeros(ms_d) # [3] for ms_key, ms_value in zip(ms_K, ms_V, strict=True): ms_S += np.outer(ms_phi(ms_key), ms_value) ms_z += ms_phi(ms_key) ms_streaming = (ms_S.T @ ms_phi(ms_q)) / (ms_z @ ms_phi(ms_q)) ms_weights = ms_phi(ms_K) @ ms_phi(ms_q) ms_traversal = (ms_weights[:, None] * ms_V).sum(0) / ms_weights.sum() # [4] assert np.allclose(ms_streaming, ms_traversal) # [5] print("streaming equals traversal:", np.allclose(ms_streaming, ms_traversal)) print(f"max |difference|: {np.abs(ms_streaming-ms_traversal).max():.3e}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` streaming equals traversal: True max |difference|: 3.469e-17 ``` ::: ::: :::: The identity is exact in real arithmetic. In floating point the two results can differ slightly, because the sums are accumulated in a different order. The traversal of the full dataset has collapsed into two running sums. With $r$ and $d_v$ fixed, storage no longer grows with the prefix. Causal **linear** attention can therefore run as a recurrence: its state stores the sufficient statistics of this regression. This construction has a limitation. Ordinary softmax's exponential dot-product kernel does not have a finite exact feature map like the one used above. With the scale $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ absorbed into $\vect{q}$, the kernel has the Taylor series $\exp(\vect{q}^{\top}\vect{k})=\sum_{m\ge0}(\vect{q}^{\top}\vect{k})^{m}/m!$. Each power $(\vect{q}^{\top}\vect{k})^{m}$ is a dot product of features built from all products of $m$ coordinates, as in $(\vect{q}^{\top}\vect{k})^{2}=\sum_{a,a'}(q_a q_{a'})(k_a k_{a'})$, so the series gives an exact feature map with such features for every $m$, infinitely many in all. Changing to a finite factorization changes the kernel, or approximates it.^[We can cut the series off after an even power, which keeps the kernel positive, or use $r$ positive features built from random projections, chosen so that $\phi(\vect{q})^{\top}\phi(\vect{k})$ equals the kernel on average over the random draw (Choromanski et al.). In both cases the relative error can rise quickly as $\norm{\vect{q}}$ and $\norm{\vect{k}}$ grow.] The state preserves the chosen kernel's readout for every query, but not the individual stored pairs: a discarded row cannot be revisited. The traversal equality is exact for the chosen factorized kernel, not a proof that finite-state linear attention reproduces exact softmax for arbitrary prefixes. ### Solver 3: take one gradient step and get the delta rule Now restrict the predictor to a scalar linear map $M(\vect{q})=\vect{h}^{\top}\vect{q}$ and let the solver take one SGD step on only the newest pair. Its instantaneous loss and gradient are $$ \ell_t(\vect{h}) =\frac{1}{2}(\vect{h}^{\top}\vect{k}_t-v_t)^2, \qquad \nabla_{\vect{h}}\ell_t =\vect{k}_t(\vect{k}_t^{\top}\vect{h}-v_t). $$ Substituting the gradient into the update gives the delta recurrence in two lines: $$ \begin{aligned} \vect{h}_t &=\vect{h}_{t-1}-\eta_t\vect{k}_t (\vect{k}_t^{\top}\vect{h}_{t-1}-v_t)\\ &=(\matr{I}-\eta_t\vect{k}_t\vect{k}_t^{\top})\vect{h}_{t-1} +\eta_t v_t\vect{k}_t. \end{aligned} $$ :::: {.plan-code} ::: {.plan} 1. Set `ms_eta` to 0.3, draw a weight vector, key, and scalar value, and compute both update forms. 2. Verify that one SGD step is the delta recurrence. 3. Print whether the two updates agree and their largest absolute difference. ::: ::: {#delta-sgd-check .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false" code-summary="Code: verify that one SGD step is the delta recurrence"} # [1] ms_eta = 0.3 ms_h = ms_rng.standard_normal(ms_d) ms_k = ms_rng.standard_normal(ms_d) ms_v = ms_rng.standard_normal() ms_sgd = ms_h - ms_eta * ms_k * (ms_k @ ms_h - ms_v) ms_delta = ((np.eye(ms_d) - ms_eta * np.outer(ms_k, ms_k)) @ ms_h + ms_eta * ms_v * ms_k) # [2] assert np.allclose(ms_sgd, ms_delta) # [3] print("SGD equals Delta recurrence:", np.allclose(ms_sgd, ms_delta)) print(f"max |difference|: {np.abs(ms_sgd-ms_delta).max():.3e}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` SGD equals Delta recurrence: True max |difference|: 4.441e-16 ``` ::: ::: :::: For vector values, store $\matr{H}_t\in\mathbb{R}^{d_v\times d_k}$, read a query as $M(\vect{q})=\matr{H}_t\vect{q}$, and replace the update by $$ \matr{H}_t =\matr{H}_{t-1} +\eta_t(\vect{v}_t-\matr{H}_{t-1}\vect{k}_t)\vect{k}_t^{\top}. $$ Each outer product writes the residual left by the current key. The update changes a query's readout in proportion to its inner product with that key, $\matr{H}_t\vect{q}-\matr{H}_{t-1}\vect{q}=\eta_t(\vect{v}_t-\matr{H}_{t-1}\vect{k}_t)(\vect{k}_t^{\top}\vect{q})$, so a query orthogonal to the key reads the same value before and after the update. DeltaNet turns that classical online least-squares step into a sequence layer. Expanding the update gives $\matr{H}_t=\matr{H}_{t-1}(\matr{I}-\eta_t\vect{k}_t\vect{k}_t^{\top})+\eta_t\vect{v}_t\vect{k}_t^{\top}$, where the transition matrix acts on the state from the right. In transposed form, $\matr{H}_t^{\top}=(\matr{I}-\eta_t\vect{k}_t\vect{k}_t^{\top})\matr{H}_{t-1}^{\top}+\eta_t\vect{k}_t\vect{v}_t^{\top}$, exposing a state-space form where $\matr{A}_t=\matr{I}-\eta_t\vect{k}_t\vect{k}_t^{\top}$ acts on the key space from the left and the input write is the outer product $\eta_t\vect{k}_t\vect{v}_t^{\top}$. The state transition is therefore determined by the current token's learned key. Exponential history weights $w_{t,\tau}=\gamma^{t-\tau}$ introduce forgetting into the least-squares *objective*, but its exact minimizer generally requires a recursive least-squares covariance state. Writing $\gamma\matr{H}_{t-1}$ into a one-step delta recurrence is a fading-memory solver choice, not an algebraic consequence of those weights. Gates can make that retention and the step size depend on the current token. Such gates link this recurrence to the wider state-space model (SSM) family (connected to the parallel-recurrence bridge of Exercise 8 of @sec-10-sequences-rnn). Mamba makes parts of its state transition, input injection, and readout depend on the token; in the regression frame, those mechanisms play roles analogous to a learnable schedule for what to keep and what to write. Gated DeltaNet adds learned gating around delta-style updates. That reading is an analogy, not a claim that Mamba is literally obtained by differentiating the shared regression objective. Structured SSMs also use different state parameterizations and can cost less, in retained state and per-token work, than the dense outer-product recurrence here. ### Retained state and per-token work {#the-price-list} ```{=html} ``` ::: {#fig-solver-costs} ::: {#830d8387 .cell fig-height='4.8' fig-width='8.8' execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](attention-as-test-time-regression_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){width=833 height=451 fig-alt='A qualitative two-axis map places three memory solvers by retained-history growth and per-token read or update cost. Softmax attention sits at growing history and growing query cost. The factorized-kernel and delta-state solvers sit at fixed retained state with dimension-dependent fixed per-token costs. Different marker shapes and direct labels identify all three.'} ::: ::: The solver map compares retained state and per-token work. Its positions are qualitative; the formulas and direct labels give the asymptotic costs for the stated dense setup. ::: The asymptotic labels in @fig-solver-costs describe this dense setup, not every implementation. Feature width $r$, head dimensions, low-rank structure, convolutions, and hardware schedules change the constants and sometimes the order of growth. ::: {.callout-warning} ## Trap: attention's memory is a dataset, not a hidden box Attention does not *have* a separate memory in the recurrent sense. The attention operation is the estimator. During causal decoding, the KV cache is the observed key--value dataset it must retain. A nonparametric query rule keeps a growing dataset so it can form a new local fit. A parametric state instead compresses those data into a fixed-size object. FlashAttention changes how the uncompressed fit is scheduled, but it does not compress the history into a fixed-size state. “Retains every row” does not mean “recalls every association without error.” Softmax still returns a convex mixture whose quality depends on keys, temperature, and interference. ::: ### Mechanism test: recall under a fixed capacity The storage comparison motivates a recall experiment to evaluate how the one-pass delta update behaves as more associations are written into a state of fixed dimension. We store $N$ random unit key--value pairs, query every stored key, and decode each retrieved vector to the nearest stored value. Exact softmax attention keeps all pairs. A dense delta state has $d^2$ numbers regardless of $N$. A selective delta arm receives one extra priority bit and writes ordinary pairs at only one-tenth strength, so the bit marks the pairs that the arm favors. We developed the study on two groups of seeds. On those groups we fixed $\eta=0.20$, the 25% priority rate, the 0.10 ordinary write gate, dimensions $(8,16,32)$, and loads $N/d\in(0.5,1,2,4,8)$. After fixing these settings, we evaluated a third, disjoint group, the held-out group, with 30 repetitions for each dimension and load. All methods in a trial receive the same keys, values, order, queries, and decoder. The code below is the frozen protocol; it runs on CPU in under a second on the reference machine. :::: {.plan-code .plan-code-wide} ::: {.plan} 1. Fix the seed, step size, ordinary write gate, three dimensions, five loads, and 30 repetitions. 2. Define the reusable helpers: `ms_unit` and `ms_decode`. 3. Define the reusable helpers: `ms_trial` and `ms_panel`. 4. Run the sealed synthetic recall-under-capacity study. ::: ::: {#memory-capacity-study .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false" code-summary="Code: run the sealed synthetic recall-under-capacity study"} # [1] MS_SEED, MS_ETA, MS_GATE = 6050, 0.20, 0.10 MS_DIMS, MS_LOADS, MS_REPEATS = (8, 16, 32), (0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8), 30 # [2] def ms_unit(x): return x / np.linalg.norm(x, axis=1, keepdims=True) def ms_decode(prediction, values): return np.argmax(prediction @ values.T, axis=1) # [3] def ms_trial(rng, repeat, d, load): n = max(4, round(load * d)) keys = ms_unit(rng.standard_normal((n, d))) values = ms_unit(rng.standard_normal((n, d))) priority = np.zeros(n, dtype=bool) priority[rng.permutation(n)[:max(1, round(0.25 * n))]] = True scores = 32.0 * (keys @ keys.T) scores -= scores.max(axis=1, keepdims=True) weights = np.exp(scores); weights /= weights.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True) attention = weights @ values def delta(write_gate): state = np.zeros((d, d)) for key, value, gate in zip(keys, values, write_gate, strict=True): state += MS_ETA * gate * np.outer(value - state @ key, key) return keys @ state.T plain = delta(np.ones(n)) selective = delta(np.where(priority, 1.0, MS_GATE)) truth = np.arange(n) correct = lambda pred: ms_decode(pred, values) == truth a_ok, d_ok, s_ok = correct(attention), correct(plain), correct(selective) ordinary = ~priority return [repeat, d, n, load, a_ok.mean(), ((attention-values)**2).mean(), d_ok.mean(), d_ok[priority].mean(), d_ok[ordinary].mean(), s_ok.mean(), s_ok[priority].mean(), s_ok[ordinary].mean()] def ms_panel(tag, repeats): seeds = np.random.SeedSequence([MS_SEED, tag]).spawn( repeats * len(MS_DIMS) * len(MS_LOADS)) rows, index = [], 0 for repeat in range(repeats): for d in MS_DIMS: for load in MS_LOADS: rows.append(ms_trial(np.random.default_rng(seeds[index]), repeat, d, load)) index += 1 return np.asarray(rows) # Tags 0 and 1 were development; tag 2 remained sealed until settings were fixed. ms_development = np.vstack([ms_panel(tag, 5) for tag in (0, 1)]) assert np.all(ms_development[:, 4] == 1.0) ms_endpoint = ms_panel(2, MS_REPEATS) assert np.all(ms_endpoint[:, 4] == 1.0) print("study_seed=6050; development_tags=(0, 1); sealed_endpoint_tag=2") print("endpoint_trials=30 x 3 dimensions; d=(8, 16, 32); " "N/d=(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8)") print("fixed: eta=0.20; priority_fraction=0.25; ordinary_write_gate=0.10") print("load attention Delta gated-all gated-priority gated-ordinary") # [4] for load in MS_LOADS: block = ms_endpoint[ms_endpoint[:, 3] == load] means = block[:, [4, 6, 9, 10, 11]].mean(0) print(f"{load:>4.1f} " + " ".join(f"{value:.3f}" for value in means)) hard = ms_endpoint[ms_endpoint[:, 3] == 8] priority_gain = hard[:, 10] - hard[:, 7] ordinary_gain = hard[:, 11] - hard[:, 8] print(f"N/d=8 gated-minus-Delta priority: {priority_gain.mean():+.3f} " f"(SD {priority_gain.std(ddof=1):.3f})") print(f"N/d=8 gated-minus-Delta ordinary: {ordinary_gain.mean():+.3f} " f"(SD {ordinary_gain.std(ddof=1):.3f})") print(f"attention top-1 failures=0/{int(ms_endpoint[:, 2].sum())}") print(f"mean value MSE={ms_endpoint[:, 5].mean():.2e}; " f"max trial MSE={ms_endpoint[:, 5].max():.2e}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` study_seed=6050; development_tags=(0, 1); sealed_endpoint_tag=2 endpoint_trials=30 x 3 dimensions; d=(8, 16, 32); N/d=(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8) fixed: eta=0.20; priority_fraction=0.25; ordinary_write_gate=0.10 load attention Delta gated-all gated-priority gated-ordinary 0.5 1.000 0.988 0.471 1.000 0.294 1.0 1.000 0.910 0.352 0.992 0.139 2.0 1.000 0.657 0.282 0.982 0.048 4.0 1.000 0.338 0.228 0.848 0.022 8.0 1.000 0.134 0.138 0.522 0.010 N/d=8 gated-minus-Delta priority: +0.387 (SD 0.156) N/d=8 gated-minus-Delta ordinary: -0.124 (SD 0.065) attention top-1 failures=0/26040 mean value MSE=5.43e-06; max trial MSE=4.55e-04 ``` ::: ::: :::: ```{=html} ``` ::: {#fig-memory-capacity-spectrum} ::: {#de4828ed .cell execution_count=7} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](attention-as-test-time-regression_files/figure-html/cell-8-output-1.png){width=818 height=333 fig-alt='Two line charts. In the left chart softmax top-1 recall stays at one while Delta recall falls with load for dimensions 8, 16, and 32. In the right chart a gated Delta update preserves priority items better than ordinary items, especially at high load, while the ungated update does not make that trade as strongly.'} ::: ::: A sealed synthetic mechanism test. The uncompressed table keeps perfect top-1 identification in this sharp-softmax construction, while the fixed delta state loses associations as $N/d$ grows. The selective arm receives a priority bit that the other arms lack and trades ordinary recall for priority recall. Keys, values, order, queries, decoder, and feature dimension $d$ are matched; stored data, side information, and inference arithmetic are not. ::: At $N/d=8$, the gate raises priority recall over the plain delta state by 0.387 on average and lowers ordinary recall by 0.124. The gate favors the retention of priority pairs at the expense of ordinary pairs, and total recall barely moves. Overall gated recall is 0.138 while plain delta recall is 0.134 at that load. Given an extra signal, a fixed state can allocate its capacity differently. These results show interference under the specified delta update as the number of stored pairs grows. They do not establish a universal recall limit for fixed-size recurrent states. Now we can compare the three solvers. Keeping the dataset provides uncompressed access at growing cost. Sufficient statistics give exact streaming evaluation for the chosen factorized kernel. Delta updates instead maintain a fixed-size predictor whose stored associations can interfere. The RNN state has returned as one of these statistical choices. ::: {.callout-note} ## Check yourself Close the book for one minute and list what each solver keeps. - Which solver retains the original key--value rows? - Why does a factorized kernel need both $\matr{S}_t$ and $\vect{z}_t$? - What information can a fixed delta state overwrite as its load grows? ::: ## Okay, so: the solver is part of the architecture 1. **The objective alone does not specify the memory system.** Views, history weights, function class, regularizer, and solver jointly define the result. 2. **Softmax attention keeps the dataset for query-dependent reads.** It preserves every key--value row, and its read cost grows with the prefix. 3. **A finite kernel feature map admits sufficient state.** The pair $(\matr{S}_t,\vect{z}_t)$ reproduces the chosen factorized-kernel traversal without retaining raw rows. 4. **One SGD step yields a delta update.** Its fixed matrix writes residuals online, which makes capacity and interference explicit. 5. **Selective retention reallocates a fixed capacity.** The sealed recall study shows a gate trading ordinary recall for priority recall, without establishing a universal architecture ranking. ## Sources and further reading {.unnumbered} - [Katharopoulos et al., *Transformers Are RNNs: Fast Autoregressive Transformers with Linear Attention*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.16236): the recurrent sufficient-state form for causal linear attention. - [Choromanski et al., *Rethinking Attention with Performers*](https://openreview.net/forum?id=Ua6zuk0WRH): positive random features whose dot product equals softmax's exponential kernel in expectation. - [Schlag, Irie, and Schmidhuber, *Linear Transformers Are Secretly Fast Weight Programmers*](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v139/schlag21a.html): the connection among linear attention, fast weights, and the delta update. - [Gu and Dao, *Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.00752): input-dependent state-space parameters, related to the regression frame by analogy rather than exact equivalence. - [Yang et al., *Gated Delta Networks: Improving Mamba2 with Delta Rule*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.06464): learned gating around delta-style associative updates. - [Wang, Shi, and Fox, *Test-Time Regression: A Unifying Framework for Designing Sequence Models with Associative Memory*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12352): the shared regression objective and solver-design perspective. - [Sun et al., *Learning to (Learn at Test Time): RNNs with Expressive Hidden States*](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/sun25h.html): a sequence model's hidden state as a learner updated by a self-supervised objective during the forward pass. - [Behrouz et al., *Titans: Learning to Memorize at Test Time*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.00663): a learned long-term memory updated at test time. - [von Oswald et al., *MesaNet: Sequence Modeling by Locally Optimal Test-Time Training*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.05233): sequence layers derived from locally solved test-time objectives. -
